title: First-yod and first-waw roots

objectives.can: Recognise forms of roots beginning with י, and of הָלַךְ, and restore the root.

explanation.summary: Roots that begin with י in the dictionary come in two kinds. Most were once roots that began with ו, and they lose that first consonant in the Qal yiqtol, imperative and infinitive, and show a ו in the Niphal and Hiphil. A few are true roots with י, and keep it. The verb הָלַךְ, 'go', is spelled differently but behaves like the first kind.

sections.heading: Where the weakness shows
body: In the Qal qatal and the Qal participle the first consonant stands at the front of the word and looks like any other: יָשַׁב, יָלַד, יָצָא, יָרַד, יֹשֵׁב. Nothing is wrong with these forms. The weakness shows when something else stands in front of the root, a prefix of the yiqtol or of a derived stem, or when the form is an imperative or an infinitive.

That is why a verb like this is easy to read in the qatal and hard to recognise in the yiqtol: the form that begins with י is not the root's י at all. In יֵצֵא the first י is the prefix of the third person, and the root's own first consonant has gone.

sections.heading: Original ו: the consonant is lost in the Qal
body: Most of these roots began with ו long ago. In the Qal yiqtol and wayyiqtol that consonant is no longer there, and the prefix has a long vowel instead: יֵשֵׁב, 'he will sit', and in the wayyiqtol וַיֵּשֶׁב, 'and he sat', with the second vowel often a segol. Other roots follow the same plan: וַיֵּצֵא from יָצָא, וַיֵּרֶד from יָרַד, וַתֵּלֶד from יָלַד, and the yiqtol forms יֵצֵא and תֵּלֵד.

The imperative also has no first consonant: שֵׁב, 'sit', רֵד, 'go down', צֵא, 'go out'. The plural keeps the same shape with a shewa under the first remaining consonant: שְׁבוּ. For יָדַע the imperative is דַּע, with a.

The infinitive construct loses the first consonant too and adds a ת ending, like the first-nun verbs: לָשֶׁבֶת, לָרֶדֶת, לָלֶדֶת. For יָצָא it is צֵאת, in forms like בְּצֵאת. The ת at the end is not a root consonant.

sections.heading: The ו that comes back in the Niphal and Hiphil
body: In the derived stems the lost consonant reappears as a vowel letter. The Niphal qatal of יָלַד is נוֹלַד, 'he was born'; the Hiphil qatal is הוֹלִיד, 'he fathered', and the Hiphil wayyiqtol is וַיּוֹלֶד. In the same way the Hiphil of יָצָא is הוֹצִיא, 'he brought out', with the first person הוֹצֵאתִי, and its wayyiqtol is וַיּוֹצֵא. The Hiphil of יָדַע is הוֹדִיעַ and of יָרַד is וַיּוֹרֶד. The Niphal of יָדַע is נוֹדַע.

The sign is a long ô (holem with ו) just before the first consonant that is left, in a form that is a Niphal or a Hiphil. When you see it, put a י in front of the remaining consonants and you have the dictionary form. The verb יָסַף is mostly met in the Hiphil, with ô or ō: וַיֹּסֶף and יֹסִיף, 'and he added', 'he adds'.

sections.heading: True י: the consonant is kept
body: A few roots really begin with י, and these keep it. The yiqtol of יָטַב is יִיטַב, with the prefix hireq and a י that follows it, and the Hiphil is written with tsere: הֵיטִיב, 'he did good', and יֵיטִיב. Compare the Hiphil of the other kind, which has ô. Similarly the yiqtol of יָרֵא has the י after the prefix: תִּירָא, 'you shall fear', אִירָא, 'I fear', and the wayyiqtol וַיִּירְאוּ.
A short form can mislead. The wayyiqtol וַיִּרְאוּ may be a form of יָרֵא, 'fear', or of רָאָה, 'see'. The two verbs have the same consonants in this form. The context and the analysis decide.
The verb יָכֹל, 'be able', has a yiqtol that looks like a passive: יוּכַל, אוּכַל, נוּכַל, תּוּכַל. These are Qal active forms, 'he can', 'I can'. Learn the shape as it is.

sections.heading: הָלַךְ, 'go'
body: The qatal and the participle of this verb begin with ה: הָלַךְ, הֹלֵךְ. In the yiqtol, the imperative and the infinitive, the ה does not appear and the verb behaves like the first kind above: יֵלֵךְ, וַיֵּלֶךְ, לֵךְ, לְכוּ, לָלֶכֶת. A reader has to know that the same verb provides both.

In this library's analysis the qatal, the participle and the infinitive absolute are filed under הָלַךְ, and the yiqtol, wayyiqtol, imperative and infinitive construct under יָלַךְ, which is the form the root takes in those forms. They are one verb in the dictionaries. The Hiphil is הוֹלִיךְ.

sections.heading: Restoring the root
body: Start with the form. If it is a Qal yiqtol or wayyiqtol whose prefix has ē and no first root consonant, put a י in front of what is left. If it is a short imperative or an infinitive ending in ת, do the same. If it is a Niphal or Hiphil with ô before the first consonant, put a י in front. If the י follows the prefix, as in יִיטַב or תִּירָא, it is a true י and belongs to the root. Then check the meaning in the verse.

misunderstandings: The י at the beginning of יֵצֵא is the prefix of the third person, not the first root consonant. The root's first consonant is not written at all.
The ו in הוֹצִיא is not a prefix or a conjunction. It is the old first consonant of the root, and it shows that the stem is a Hiphil of a root that began with י.
The final ת of לָשֶׁבֶת and לָלֶדֶת does not belong to the root; it is the ending of the infinitive.
Not every verb that has י in its dictionary form loses it. יָטַב and יָרֵא keep it, and their forms look quite different from those of יָשַׁב.

deeper.heading: Why a י written for an old ו
body: Hebrew at an earlier stage seems to have had many roots beginning with a ו sound. At the front of a word that sound became י in the Qal qatal, and the older ו survives in the Niphal and Hiphil where it is inside the word. This is the usual account in the old grammars; for reading, all you need is the pattern.
